Issued at 302 PM EST Sun Nov 8 2026

Afternoon GOES water vapor imagery reveals a sharp shortwave trough 
digging across northern Ontario with the attendant surface low 
pressure reflection further north towards James Bay. A cold front 
has passed SE of the UP this morning, ushering in modest cold air 
advection and pressure rises that has contributed to gusty NW winds 
25-45 mph, highest in the Keweenaw and over Lake Superior. 
Additionally, 850mb temps near 0 to -2C have supported blustery lake 
enhanced showers across the area, mainly the east half given the 
northwesterly fetch. Continued NW flow behind the departing will 
support these conditions for the remainder of the day before 
gradually tapering off tonight as a brief ridge and weak high 
pressure settle atop the region by Monday morning. Overnight temps 
fall into the 30s and 40s, warmest lakeshores. Another clipper, 
albeit more low amplitude, presses north of Lake Superior through 
Monday PM, bringing an uptick in SW winds and climbing temps into 
the upper 40s to low 50s, some 5-10 degrees above normal for this 
time of year. With the greatest forcing for ascent remaining north 
of the UP, thinking it should be a dry day, though can't rule out a 
light isolated shower in the east (<20%). Dry conditions hold 
through Tuesday as the clipper passes northeast of the Upper Great 
Lakes, veering breezy winds westerly and keeping one more day of 
above normal temps.

The more fun and challenging forecast presents itself during the 
latter half of this week as a closed upper low in the Canadian 
maritime provinces and far northern Quebec slowly retrogrades SW 
towards James Bay/western Quebec while several additional shortwaves 
round the far western base of the trough straight south across 
Ontario through the Great Lakes. In turn, this creates a somewhat 
prolonged period of northerly flow across Lake Superior, bringing 
down 850 mb temps between -7 to -11C Wednesday night through 
Saturday. Lake effect precipitation will begin to occur Wednesday 
afternoon as temps aloft cool to the 8-13C delta T before becoming 
all lake effect snow late into Thursday morning. LES persists across 
the north wind snowbelts through at least Saturday morning. Some 
appreciable snow accumulations may be on the horizon if necessary 
ingredients come together. Bufkit soundings in the N wind snowbelts 
suggest ample moisture in the lower levels but lack saturation 
within the DGZ, leading to lower SLRs and thus wetter snow 
character. I suspect this may be a little underdone and lake 
enhanced inversion heights upwards of 6-9 kft may be able to provide 
additional moisture into the DGZ. Within the broad northerly flow 
aloft, several shortwave pivoting through the Upper Great Lakes may 
be able to help boost localized convergence over the lake and thus 
help drive dominant band structures that are capable of producing 
locally heavier snowfall. Plus, with an unfrozen Lake Nipigon to the 
north, seeder-feeder action from Nipigon may also help play a role 
in dominant banding into the central UP. Given the warm lake temp 
average near +9C, I also suspect the greatest snowfall accumulations 
will be found, as per usual, in the higher terrain of the Michigamme 
Highlands of Marquette and Baraga counties where the lake modified 
airmass is harder to penetrate and terrain enhancement occurs the 
best. Temps should be cold enough to allow snow to fall at the 
immediate lakeshores, but warm lake-modifed air, less frictional 
convergence, and gusty northerly winds 15-25 kts will displace the 
best totals inland. The latest ensemble guidance is trending upward 
in terms of snow totals, with the latest NBM suggesting a 40% chance 
48 hr totals >4" in the central UP high terrain ending Saturday 
night. The Euro Ens paints a 50-70% chance for at least 6" across 
the same area/timeframe. Given how poor the NBM handles LES, it 
wouldn't shock me to see the total/probs increase over the next few 
cycles.
